Executive Summary: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia in October damaged data centers operated by Yandex, VK, Sberbank, and Russia’s Federal Tax Service, disrupting digital services and prompting discussion of relocating infrastructure from the Moscow region to the Far East. Moscow is moving to formalize its artificial intelligence (AI) policy as concerns grow that Russian systems are falling behind U.S. and Chinese models. New AI legislation entered into force in September. Russian officials view domestic AI as a matter of national sovereignty, but shortages of computing infrastructure and skilled personnel, alongside growing use of foreign AI models, threaten Moscow’s efforts to develop a competitive domestic sector. Ukrainian drone strikes on October 8 struck one of the large data centers belonging to Yandex, Russia’s largest tech company, leading to massive interruptions in the company’s services around the country. The strikes pushed the company’s cloud services into emergency mode, and clients had to move their data to other cloud systems ( Habr , October 12). Other services within the Yandex digital ecosystem required weeks to recover ( T-J , October 26). VK Company Limited—another major tech company which controls the leading Russian-language social media sites VKontakte and Odnoklassniki, the national messaging system Max, and Mail.ru, Russia’s leading e-mail service—also recently faced damage to its data centers, as did Sberbank, Russia’s largest financial institution ( CNews , October 18). These attacks underscore just one of the many difficulties facing the Kremlin as it continues to push for complete digital sovereignty. These October attacks fit into a broader pattern of Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian data centers, including those belonging to federal organizations, such as the National Tax Service in Nizhnyi Novgorod ( Nastoyashee Vremya , October 23). Ozon, an e-commerce company that is considered Russia’s answer to Amazon, has faced continued drone attacks targeting their warehouses since August ( Omskinform , October 28).  The attacks have had serious consequences for Russia’s attempts to develop a secure and sovereign tech sector. The Russian technology industry is calling for additional security, and some are discussing potentially relocating data centers to the Far East, as 75 percent of commercial data centers are currently located in Moscow oblast ( Techora , October 27). Other options discussed in the technology press include moving data centers to Kazakhstan. Yandex has not faced comprehensive Western sanctions, enabling it to potentially move infrastructure abroad ( Habr , October 12). The physical attacks on Russia’s technology sector come as the Kremlin becomes more concerned about the future of artificial intelligence (AI) in the country. The Russian Duma formed a committee to address AI issues, headed by Aleksandr Sidyakin, deputy secretary general of the ruling United Russia party and one of the initiators of Russia’s “foreign agents” law, which nominally aimed to reduce foreign influence in the country and suppressed independent media, non-governmental organizations, and non-systemic political opposition ( Meduza , September 24). Russian President Vladimir Putin has said that Russia’s sovereignty will depend on the country’s ability to develop its own domestic AI ( RBC , April 10). The rapid development of AI use in Russia’s war against Ukraine has completely altered the battlefield, reducing the applicability of lessons from previous wars, according to Russian Deputy Defense Minister General Yunus-Bek Evkurov in an August interview ( RBC , August 10). The first legislation specifying Kremlin policies for the development of domestic models entered into effect in September, though some provisions will not take effect until March 2027. “Sovereign” AI models must use only domestic technologies under the law, while “national” models can use foreign components and open-source solutions ( RBC , August 31). “Sovereign” models, according to Sidyakin, must “conform to Russian spiritual and moral values” ( RIA Novosti , October 27). Moscow is concerned that Russian AI is falling behind models from the United States and the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Sberbank President German Gref estimated that Russian AI was a half-year behind Beijing’s systems and expressed fears that this lag will continue ( RBC , September 24). This announcement followed news that PRC models were the second and third most popular models among Russian clients using domestic cloud platforms, with the use of PRC AI growing elevenfold year-on-year ( Kommersant , August 13). Surveys published in the summer found that respondents from 79 percent of 100 major Russian companies reported too few AI specialists and 91 percent lacked sufficient server infrastructure ( ITZine , July 29).  These concerns about AI development are compounded by evidence of brain drain. Arkadii Volozh, the original founder of Yandex, immigrated to the Netherlands in 2024 after criticizing Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, taking 1,000 engineers with him, along with plans to develop a company specializing in infrastructure for AI systems. His assets were then sold to Russian investors for $5.4 billion ( IncRussia , July 16). The Kremlin is subsidizing the development of domestic AI by offering tax breaks to small and medium enterprises that adopt domestic solutions, but the country will need 89,000 AI specialists by 2030, according to estimates presented at a tech conference by former Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitrii Gorgenko ( Vedomosti , September 21; Ekspert , October 24). The new AI legislation is part of a broader shift toward Russian digital sovereignty. This push includes a “sovereign” internet and national network defense system (see EDM , May 20). Russia faces serious challenges, including developing national AI systems that can compete with U.S. and PRC versions while protecting its technology infrastructure from Ukrainian strikes. Further attacks leading to extended online interruptions would likely undermine support for the war effort and disrupt Russia’s digital economy. A major relocation of technology infrastructure to the Far East would likely require heavy state support and the development of an ecosystem to support the data centers, both serious undertakings for an economy that is facing stagnation (see EDM , November 2).  The post Russia’s Push for AI Sovereignty Faces Setbacks appeared first on Jamestown .

title: Keep US troops in NATO’s KFOR
zh_title: 让美军留在北约驻科部队
summary: 随着五角大楼最终完成对美国在欧洲的军事态势的审查，一项相对较小的承诺值得避免预算削减：即在北约科索沃部队服役的约 600 名美国士兵。他们几乎没有参与关于旅和数十亿美元项目的辩论，但他们在巴尔干地区保持了来之不易的和平，将他们撤出几乎什么也挽救不了，同时让莫斯科获得了廉价的战略胜利。驻科部队于 1999 年 6 月在北约指挥下部署，此前该联盟轰炸了南斯拉夫，以制止斯洛博丹·米洛舍维奇的塞尔维亚军队对 A 族人实施的暴力行为
content:
随着五角大楼最终完成对美国在欧洲的军事态势的审查，一项相对较小的承诺值得避免预算削减：即在北约科索沃部队服役的约 600 名美国士兵。他们几乎没有参与关于旅和数十亿美元项目的辩论，但他们在巴尔干地区保持了来之不易的和平，将他们撤出几乎什么也挽救不了，同时让莫斯科获得了廉价的战略胜利。驻科部队于 1999 年 6 月在北约指挥下部署，此前北约轰炸了南斯拉夫，以制止斯洛博丹·米洛舍维奇领导的塞尔维亚军队对阿尔巴尼亚人的暴力行为。科索沃于2008年宣布独立，但塞尔维亚在俄罗斯和中国的支持下仍然拒绝承认。欧洲态势评估是一项合法的活动。在多年来敦促欧洲盟国承担更多常规防御之后，特朗普政府正确地提出了一些尖锐的问题，即美国军队在哪些方面可以增加独特的价值，以及在适当的时间发展其能力和能力的情况下欧洲可以在哪些方面加强。但驻科部队是一项美国角色不易被取代的任务，因为它既是政治性的，也是军事性的，而且错误的决定可能会导致欧洲东南侧的不稳定。从威胁开始。即使在乌克兰遭受重大损失的同时，弗拉基米尔·普京也没有放弃破坏欧洲稳定的努力。巴尔干地区是欧洲的软肋，是一个备受青睐的舞台：煽动成本低廉，是一个分散西方对乌克兰注意力的地方。
莫斯科长期以来一直利用塞尔维亚作为破坏科索沃稳定的杠杆。2017年，一列俄罗斯制造的火车开往科索沃北部，这是一次带有“科索沃是塞尔维亚”口号的滚动挑衅。俄罗斯在科索沃附近运营着一个所谓的人道主义中心，该中心被怀疑充当俄罗斯情报站。塞尔维亚与俄罗斯密切的情报联系使莫斯科能够接触到准备挑衅的当地民族主义力量。 2023年，科索沃北部警察遭到武装袭击，普里什蒂纳将此归咎于塞尔维亚支持的武装分子，这加剧了人们对与俄罗斯结盟的行为体利用紧张局势的担忧；今年早些时候，俄罗斯外交部长警告称，“欧洲中心正在酝酿一场重大爆炸性局势”。紧张局势一再爆发。 2023年5月，塞尔维亚抗议者与科索沃警察发生冲突，造成90多名北约维和人员受伤，促使塞尔维亚提高军事戒备级别。那年 9 月，在巴尼斯卡发生的一次袭击中，全副武装的塞族枪手杀死了一名科索沃警察，并将自己关在一座修道院里，这表明当地的冲突可以多么迅速地演变为地区危机。危险还没有过去。塞尔维亚强人亚历山大·武契奇承认在10月25日的塞尔维亚议会选举中落败，但贝尔格莱德的外交政策方向尚不确定，人们担心其对科索沃的看法不会改变。
十月，俄罗斯驻联合国大使警告说，科索沃局势“仍然持续紧张，甚至濒临崩溃”。尽管如此，科索沃和塞尔维亚自 1999 年以来一直保持和平，这在很大程度上要归功于驻科部队。用美国两党议员团体的话说，这支部队的作用是“对那些试图煽动种族暴力的人起到政治威慑作用”。美国从驻科部队撤军可能会助长科索沃和塞尔维亚的民族主义议程，以及波斯尼亚附近塞族统治地区塞族共和国的分裂主义野心。美国在驻科部队中的存在之所以受到重视，正是因为

【原文 English Original】
As the Pentagon finalizes its review of U.S. force posture in Europe, one relatively small commitment deserves protection from the budget axe: the roughly 600 American troops serving in NATO’s Kosovo Force. They barely register in a debate about brigades and billion-dollar line items, but they keep a hard-won peace in the Balkans, and pulling them out would save almost nothing while handing Moscow a cheap strategic win. KFOR was deployed in June 1999 under NATO command, after the alliance bombed Yugoslavia to stop the violence perpetrated by Slobodan Milosevic’s Serbian forces against ethnic Albanians. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, but Serbia, backed by Russia and China, still refuses to recognize it. The Europe posture review is a legitimate exercise. After years of urging European allies to shoulder more of their own conventional defense, the Trump administration is right to ask hard questions about where American forces add unique value and where Europe can step up given suitable time to develop their capabilities and capacities. But KFOR is a mission in which the American role is not easily replaced, because it is as much political as military, and where a wrong call risks instability on Europe’s southeastern flank. Start with the threat. Even while absorbing heavy losses in Ukraine, Vladimir Putin has not given up on destabilizing Europe. The Balkans, Europe’s soft underbelly, are a favored arena: cheap to stir, a place to distract Western attention from Ukraine. Moscow has long used Serbia as a lever against Kosovo’s stability. In 2017, a Russian-made train was sent toward northern Kosovo, a rolling provocation that bore the slogan “Kosovo is Serbia.” Russia runs a so-called humanitarian center near Kosovo that is suspected of serving as a Russian intelligence station. Close Serbian-Russian intelligence ties give Moscow access to local nationalist forces prepared for provocations. In 2023, an armed attack on Kosovo police in the north, which Pristina blamed on Serbian-backed militants, heightened fears that Russian-aligned actors were exploiting the tension; earlier that year, Russia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs warned that “a major explosive situation is brewing in the heart of Europe.” Tensions have repeatedly flared. In May 2023, clashes between Serb protesters and Kosovo police injured more than 90 NATO peacekeepers and prompted Serbia to raise its military alert level. That September, an attack in Banjska, where heavily armed Serb gunmen killed a Kosovo police officer and barricaded themselves in a monastery, showed how quickly a local flare-up can become a regional crisis. The danger has not passed. Serbian strongman Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Serbia’s Oct. 25 parliamentary election, but Belgrade’s foreign-policy direction is uncertain and there are concerns that its views on Kosovo will not change. In October, Russia’s ambassador to the UN warned that the situation in Kosovo “remains persistently tense and is literally teetering on the brink.” Still, Kosovo and Serbia have remained at peace since 1999, in large part because of KFOR. In the words of a bipartisan group of U.S lawmakers, the force functions as “a political deterrent to those seeking to stoke ethnic violence.” An American drawdown from KFOR may embolden nationalist agendas in Kosovo and Serbia as well as separatist ambitions in Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated region in nearby Bosnia. The American presence in KFOR is valued precisely because it is American. U.S. troops have anchored KFOR since its creation, and Washington currently leads Regional Command East, a position of real operational weight, not symbolism. The U.S. has traditionally provided the 600 or so American troops—often Army National Guardsmen—an economy-of-force mission with minimal cost or effect on the U.S. Army’s ability to execute missions elsewhere around the globe. The mission accounts for less than 1 percent of the total U.S. troops in Europe. KFOR’s value becomes plain when contrasted with Operation Althea in neighboring Bosnia. EUFOR, an EU-led force with roughly 1,500 troops, has struggled to respond decisively to repeated provocations by Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik, who’s backed by Moscow and Belgrade. EU ambassadors rejected Bosnian appeals to help enforce an arrest warrant against him in 2025, citing political risk. Dodik has openly mocked EUFOR’s patrols. Lacking an American anchor and a unified chain of command willing to act, EUFOR has too often had to manage crises rather than deterring them. KFOR, by contrast, has demonstrated it can surge forces when tested, providing genuine deterrence. After the 2023 Banjska incident, NATO increased its peacekeeping presence in Kosovo. Serbia drew down its border deployment, ending the crisis. The Pentagon is right to ask what the value of an American military presence is worth. For KFOR, the answer is plain: a few hundred U.S. troops are successfully maintaining a quarter-century-long peace that Russia would love to see unravel. Lawmakers from both parties already understand that. The Pentagon should, too, and keep KFOR intact. Mark Montgomery, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral, serves as a senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ (FDD), where Ivana Stradner is a research fellow. ]]>

title: RISC-V Open-Source Chip Push Puts Strategy Over Capability
zh_title: RISC-V 开源芯片的推动将战略置于能力之上
summary: 内容摘要：中华人民共和国 (PRC) 正在扩大对 RISC-V（一种开源芯片设计标准）的使用，并扩大其对管理该标准的国际非营利组织的影响力。近年来，人们越来越担心被切断与 Arm 和英特尔等西方行业领导者设计的芯片的联系。中国公司现在不仅为消费设备而且为服务器和数据中心制造 RISC-V 芯片，尽管它们的功能不如专有芯片。 V100 于 10 月推出，由国家支持的实体共同创建，被宣传为首款
content:
内容摘要：中华人民共和国 (PRC) 正在扩大对 RISC-V（一种开源芯片设计标准）的使用，并扩大其对管理该标准的国际非营利组织的影响力。近年来，人们越来越担心被切断与 Arm 和英特尔等西方行业领导者设计的芯片的联系。中国公司现在不仅为消费设备而且为服务器和数据中心制造 RISC-V 芯片，尽管它们的功能不如专有芯片。 V100于10月推出，由国家支持的实体共同创建，号称是首款完全符合RISC-V服务器标准的通用芯片。国家级政策文件传统上避免直接讨论RISC-V，但今年9月，《电子信息制造业“十五五”规划》宣布，要求推进RISC-V研发和产业化，开发人工智能（AI）RISC-V芯片。 RISC-V 为自力更生带来了明显的好处，并且芯片可以进行调整，包括针对军事用例进行优化。
然而，中国的分析师担心芯片的“玻璃天花板”，甚至国家 IT 替代计划也指出，在政府系统中用于替代外国技术的 RISC-V 芯片的份额“可以忽略不计”。 10月19日，深圳芯片制造商进迭时空与香山处理器团队在第六届RISC-V中国峰会上推出了新型46核服务器芯片V100。[1]其制造商宣称其是首款完全符合RISC-V服务器标准的通用芯片（21世纪经济报道，10月19日；科技日报，10月20日）。 RISC-V 是一种开源指令集架构 (ISA)，是处理器运行的语言。与全球几乎所有计算机和手机中使用的 Arm 或 Intel x86 等专有 ISA 不同，任何人都可以使用 RISC-V，无需支付许可费或需要其他权限。由英国和美国公司制造的 Arm 和英特尔处理器必须遵守这些国家政府实施的许可和出口管制。相比之下，RISC-V 主要由 RISC-V International 监管，这是一家总部位于瑞士的非营利组织，旨在避免此类漏洞。最近推出的服务器芯片代表了中华人民共和国（PRC）该行业更广泛的趋势。
北京最初在 2010 年代中期开始将 RISC-V 视为对抗西方技术霸权并扩大其在新兴技术领域结构性力量的一种方式（中国简报，2023 年 12 月 15 日）。此后，北京通过国家主导的政策支持鼓励其发展，从城市层面开始，逐步上升到国家层面。尽管这些芯片的功能仍然落后于西方竞争对手，但它们越来越多地部署在数据中心的服务器中，而不仅仅是嵌入消费设备中。从市政厅到五年计划 2023年以来，地方层面对RISC-V的支持已经明确，特别是在上海、北京和深圳等一线城市（中国简报，2023年12月15日）。北京经济技术开发区的目标是到 2030 年使 RISC-V 产业价值超过 500 亿元人民币（70 亿美元），据一些估计，届时全国市场将达到约 2200 亿元人民币（210 亿美元）（北京市政府，2025 年 1 月 3 日；中国日报）

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: The People’s Republic of China (PRC) is expanding its use of RISC-V, an open-source chip design standard, as well as its influence over the international nonprofit organization that manages it. This follows growing fears in recent years of being cut off from chips designed by Western industry leaders such as Arm and Intel. PRC firms are now creating RISC-V chips not just for consumer devices but for servers and data centers, even though they are less powerful than proprietary chips. The V100, launched in October and co-created by a state-backed entity, is billed as the first general-purpose chip fully compliant with RISC-V server standards. National-level policy documents have traditionally avoided discussing RISC-V directly, but in September, the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Electronic Information Manufacturing Industry announced calls to advance RISC-V research, development, and industrialization, and to develop RISC-V chips for artificial intelligence (AI). RISC-V brings clear benefits for self-reliance, and the chips can be adapted, including being optimized for military use cases. Analysts in the PRC worry, however, about a “glass ceiling” for the chips, and even the state IT substitution program has noted that the share of RISC-V chips it has used to replace foreign technology in government systems is “negligible.” On October 19, Shenzhen-based chipmaker SpacemiT (进迭时空) and the state-backed XiangShan (香山) processor team launched the V100, a new 46-core server chip, at the sixth RISC-V Summit China.  [1] Its makers bill it as the first general-purpose chip fully compliant with RISC-V server standards ( 21st Century Business Herald , October 19; Science and Technology Daily , October 20). RISC-V is an open-source instruction set architecture (ISA), which is the language that processors run on. Unlike proprietary ISAs, such as Arm or Intel’s x86 that are used in almost all of the world’s computers and phones, anyone can use RISC-V without paying a license fee or requiring other permissions. Arm and Intel processors, made by British and U.S. companies, must abide by licensing and export controls put in place by those countries’ governments. By comparison, RISC-V is mainly overseen by RISC-V International, a Switzerland-based nonprofit that avoids such vulnerabilities. The recently unveiled server chip is representative of broader trends in the sector within the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Beijing initially began to view RISC-V as a way to counter the West’s technological hegemony and extend its structural power in emerging technologies in the mid-2010s ( China Brief , December 15, 2023). Since then, it has encouraged its development through state-led policy support, starting at the city level and moving up to the national level. Although the chips’ capabilities remain behind those of Western rivals, they are increasingly being deployed in servers for data centers, not just embedded in consumer devices. From City Halls to the Five-Year Plan Since 2023, local-level support for RISC-V has been explicit, especially in first-tier cities like Shanghai, Beijing, and Shenzhen ( China Brief , December 15, 2023). Beijing’s Economic-Technological Development Area aims for a RISC-V industry worth more than renminbi (RMB) 50 billion ($7 billion) by 2030, at which point the national market will reach around RMB 220 billion ($21 billion), according to some estimates ( Beijing Municipal Government , January 3, 2025; China Daily , October 22). National-level documents have tended instead to use the term “open source” to implicitly refer to RISC-V. In mid-September, however, the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Electronic Information Manufacturing Industry announced calls to “advance the research, development, and industrialization of RISC-V” (推进第五代精简指令集 (RISC-V) 研发与产业化), and to support RISC-V artificial intelligence (AI) and embedded system chips ( Ministry of Information and Industry Technology , September 15).  [2] Server Ambitions, Smartphone-Class Silicon RISC-V’s strength so far has been in cheaper control chips for appliances and cars, but newer chips signal data center servers as an emerging use case. The Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) calls the open-source XiangShan core the most powerful of its kind in the world ( China Daily , March 26). Beyond the latest processor from SpacemiT and XiangShan, Alibaba now offers a server-class design, the C950, that it says performs on par with Apple’s M1 chip, which it released in 2020, on a standard performance test ( The Register , March 25). Engineers usually judge how well a core is designed via a two-step process. First, they run an industry-standard test, which times how long a processor takes to complete a set of tasks, and turns that time into a score. Second, they divide the score by the core’s clock speed, which is the number of steps it takes each second, measured in gigahertz (GHz). The result measures how much work a core does in each step (see Figure 1). On this metric, PRC progress is substantial: XiangShan’s cores have roughly doubled since 2021. (Sources: Apple , May 7, 2024; AMD , June 2, 2024; Intel , October 10, 2024; Nvidia, January 16, 2025 , accessed November 3 ; Microsoft , December 19, 2025; SpacemiT , September 24; Qualcomm , accessed November 3). RISC-V Buys Assurance and Customization RISC-V offers the PRC with two benefits: the assurance of sustainable access, and adaptability for military purposes, which would be risky use-cases for employing Western chips. The fear of being cut off from access to chips has been acute since Huawei learned in 2019 that its access to Arm’s designs could be suspended ( BBC , May 22, 2019). As an open-source architecture, RISC-V can be modified and tailored to user requirements. In some instances, however, this has allowed it to be adapted for military purposes. A team at Information Engineering University, an institution affiliated with the People’s Liberation Army, was able to customize command for data encryption to a small RISC-V chip, accelerating encryption by about seven times with only about two percent more circuitry.  [5] These benefits are another part of the reason why the PRC has pushed to deepen its influence over RISC-V at the international level. Chinese firms now hold half of the 24 top-tier memberships in RISC-V International ( RISC-V , accessed November 3). U.S. firms are deepening their stake in the RISC-V ecosystem too. Nvidia said in July 2025 that its CUDA software, the backbone of AI computing, would support RISC-V processors, and Qualcomm bought the RISC-V server designer Ventana in December 2025 ( The Register , July 21, 2025; Qualcomm , December 10, 2025). Conclusion Beijing continues to emphasize RISC-V to advance technological self-reliance and resilience. Although it is starting to use RISC-V chips in servers and data centers, the chips function at well below the capabilities of the most advanced processors. Analysts in the PRC have worried about a “glass ceiling” (玻璃天花板) for the chips, and even the state IT substitution program (信创) has noted that the share of RISC-V chips it has used to replace foreign technology in government systems is “negligible (微乎其微)” ( Sina Finance , April 7). It is nevertheless too soon to dismiss the hype over the PRC’s RISC-V development. RISC-V currently also enjoys support from U.S. companies. This makes the international standards that govern RISC-V an important battle ground in the competition to shape this arena of open-source technology. It remains unclear, however, whether the United States will seek to build a U.S.-led ISA ecosystem or discourage U.S. and allied firms from taking part in Chinese-led RISC-V projects. Neither option is cost-free, although if Washington does not take action, a key part of the semiconductor supply chain could end up being controlled by Beijing. Notes [1] A core is the part of a processor that reads and carries out software instructions. [2] The plan was released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the National Development and Reform Commission, but grew out of work by eight agencies that drafted the country’s first national guidance on RISC-V in 2025 ( Reuters , March 3, 2025). [3] For Figure 2, panel A estimates the real speed of a single core by multiplying its points per gigahertz by the clock speed at which it actually ships, and shows the result relative to a core in Nvidia’s Grace server processor (set at 100). Intel and AMD do not publish comparable SPECint2006 figures, so their desktop cores are set equal to Arm’s Cortex-X925, which independent testing by Chips and Cheese found to be within the margin of error of the fastest AMD and Intel cores on the newer SPECint2017 test ( Chips and Cheese, March 3 ). Panels B and C compare whole server chips. The first is the number of cores. Each core works on its own task, so more cores means more work at once. The second is memory speed, or bandwidth: how many gigabytes of data a chip can move to and from its memory each second. In large data-center jobs this is often the real limit, because even a fast core sits idle while it waits for data. The lower panels of Figure 2 compare other measures of performance for entire server chips. The V100 has 46 cores; Nvidia’s Grace has 72; and the top Intel and AMD server chips have 128–192. The V100 also moves data to and from memory at about half their speed. It draws far less power, however, at 120 watts, compared to about 250 for Grace and 500 for the Intel and AMD chips ( GitHub , accessed October 27). [4] Figure 3 measures AI performance in trillions of simple calculations per second (TOPS). Since AI models run on vast numbers of such calculations, higher TOPS values translate to faster AI. The left panel divides TOPS by the power a chip draws, in watts, to show energy efficiency, which matters most in battery-powered robots and drones. The right panel shows raw TOPS for laptop chips. Companies quote TOPS in different ways that can double or even quadruple the headline number, so the chart puts every chip on the same basis. Even if the SpacemiT processor reaches 30 TOPS, this is still short of Microsoft’s bar of 40. By The Register’s estimate, even Alibaba’s best design would roughly match Apple’s M1 ( The Register , March 25). [5] Zhang Xiaolei, Dai Zibin, Guo Pengfei, et al., “Design and Verification of a RISC-V-Based AES Cryptographic Acceleration Engine [基于RISC-V的AES密码加速引擎设计与验证],” Application of Electronic Technique [电子技术应用] 49, no. 2 (2023): 39–44. Results are from FPGA prototypes built on the open-source Hummingbird E203 core. The post RISC-V Open-Source Chip Push Puts Strategy Over Capability appeared first on Jamestown .

Chinese v American Views on WAR with Taiwan
Posted Aug 14, 2026 by Martin Armstrong |
The Center for Strategic and International Studies conducted an extraordinary survey of 64 leading experts on China, Taiwan, and cross-Strait relations, including 28 former senior U.S. government officials, 23 former government policy and intelligence analysts, and 13 academics and think-tank experts. What their answers reveal is not that China is preparing to invade Taiwan tomorrow, as the neocons would like everyone to believe, but that Beijing remains willing to wait so long as nobody crosses the line of formal Taiwanese independence. Some 84% said Beijing is willing to wait for unification but will not accept the status quo permanently, while only 10% believed China seeks unification at the earliest opportunity. Not one of the 64 experts believed Beijing would ever accept an independent Taiwan.
This is precisely why Taiwan has become so dangerous. The West keeps portraying the conflict as if Xi Jinping wakes up every morning staring at a calendar trying to decide when to launch an amphibious invasion. Yet 83% of these experts said China did not plan to use significant kinetic force against Taiwan by 2027, and 80% said China’s enormous 2022 military exercises did not indicate Beijing had accelerated its timetable. Only 6% of respondents outside the former senior government group saw 2027 as a hard deadline, while not one former senior U.S. official did. The obsession with 2027 has nevertheless become extremely useful for the military establishment because every supposed deadline becomes another justification for weapons, deployments, bases, and spending.
The survey found that 44% believed Beijing has a hard deadline of 2049, the centennial of the People’s Republic, while 42% believed China could wait indefinitely provided unification remains possible. This is an important distinction because China thinks in terms of generations while Western politicians think in terms of the next election. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan if economic, political, and military pressure can gradually change the situation in its favor. Only 20% of those surveyed believed China even possessed a coherent roadmap for peaceful unification, which tells us this is not some perfectly scripted invasion plan sitting in Xi’s desk drawer.
Where the numbers become alarming is not an unprovoked invasion but what happens when politicians begin crossing China’s red lines. More than three-quarters of the experts, 77%, believed China would invade within six months if Taiwan formally declared independence. Among former senior U.S. officials, that number was 79%. Even some of those who did not expect an immediate invasion believed Beijing would respond with a blockade or enormous military exercises. This is why politicians encouraging Taiwan toward formal independence are playing with the lives of 23 million people. They can deliver all the speeches they want about democracy from Washington, London, or Brussels, but they will not be the civilians sitting underneath the missiles if their political experiment goes wrong.
Not one expert believed an explicit American commitment to defend Taiwan would cause China to invade immediately, but 64% believed Beijing would respond strongly enough to provoke a U.S.-China or China-Taiwan crisis, while another 31% expected a more limited negative response. Only two of the 64 experts believed formally committing America to Taiwan’s defense would actually deter China from using force because Beijing already assumes that the United States will intervene anyway.
A direct invasion is not even the most likely path toward conflict. Only 8% of the experts described an amphibious invasion within ten years as likely, while 63% called it possible and 27% unlikely. Force short of invasion received much higher probabilities, with 52% saying deliberate escalation such as a blockade was likely or very likely. An accidental military incident was considered even more dangerous, with 34% saying a collision or accident around the Taiwan Strait was likely and another 22% calling it very likely. When warships and aircraft from opposing nuclear powers continually operate around the same small body of water, war does not require some grand master plan. It requires one mistake followed by politicians who refuse to back down.
A later CSIS survey of American and Taiwanese experts reinforces that point. Roughly 90% of U.S. experts and 62% of Taiwanese experts believed China already possessed the capability to impose a law-enforcement-led quarantine that substantially reduces trade into Taiwan. Around 80% of American experts and 60% of Taiwanese experts believed Beijing could execute a PLA blockade, while Taiwanese experts were considerably more skeptical that China could successfully carry out an invasion. If Beijing wanted to coerce Taiwan during the following five years, experts considered a quarantine the most likely option. If China decided it wanted immediate unification, however, approximately 80% regarded a highly kinetic joint blockade as likely or very likely.
This is where the economic consequences become enormous because Taiwan does not need to be invaded for the world economy to be thrown into chaos. A quarantine or blockade would immediately threaten shipping, insurance, semiconductor supply chains, electronics, automobiles, communications equipment, and virtually every modern industry dependent upon advanced chips. The later CSIS survey found most American and Taiwanese experts did not believe Taiwan could withstand a Chinese blockade for longer than three months without substantial U.S. intervention. Washington would then face the decision nobody wants to discuss honestly: accept China’s blockade or attempt to break it militarily and risk direct war between two nuclear powers.
Taiwan is also the world’s semiconductor pressure point. The island’s importance to advanced chip manufacturing means a serious blockade would not remain a regional event. Factories thousands of miles away could discover that a conflict they thought had nothing to do with them suddenly prevents them from obtaining critical components. Markets would begin repricing the risk immediately, shipping premiums would explode, companies would scramble for inventory, and governments would discover once again how fragile global supply chains have become. This is why capital will react long before politicians formally declare that a war has begun.
What I find particularly revealing in the later CSIS survey is the difference between American confidence and Taiwanese confidence in Washington. An astonishing 96% of American experts were completely or moderately confident that the United States would intervene militarily if China invaded Taiwan during the following five years. Taiwanese experts were less confident in American intervention and considerably less confident that U.S. allies would join the fight. It is always easier for people thousands of miles away to be certain about somebody else’s war.
This is precisely why Taiwan remains one of the critical geopolitical pressure points as we move toward 2029. The danger is not simply that China arbitrarily decides to invade. The greater danger is escalation, miscalculation, political promises that cannot be withdrawn, and Western policymakers convincing themselves that every additional provocation somehow produces deterrence. China has made its position on formal independence perfectly clear, and even the experts inside the Western foreign-policy establishment overwhelmingly acknowledge that Beijing would react with force if that line were crossed.
If Taiwan declares formal independence, 77% of the experts surveyed believed China would invade within six months. That is not a statistic policymakers should treat as another war-game scenario. It is a warning about what happens when politicians deliberately remove the ambiguity that has helped keep the peace.

title: Labour Dept warns employers, workers on electrical safety in rain
zh_title: 劳工部警告雇主和工人雨天用电安全
summary: 劳工部警告雇主、工人雨天用电安全中国劳工布告栏 星期六, 14 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻英文版 劳工部警告雇主、工人雨天用电安全 香港劳工处敦促雇主和承包商避免指派工人在受雨影响的地区进行电力工作，即使在潮湿的干燥地点，也要遵守安全准则。措施包括隔离电源、使用防护装备以及在 2026 年 11 月 14 日香港时间 03:56 之前进行风险评估 · 更新于 11 月 14 日 04:24 · 2 分钟准备
content:
劳工部警告雇主、工人雨天用电安全中国劳工公告栏
星期六, 14 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻英文版
劳工部警告雇主和工人雨天用电安全
香港劳工处敦促雇主和承包商避免指派工人在雨灾地区进行电力工作，即使在潮湿的干燥地点，也要遵守安全准则。措施包括隔离电源、使用防护装备以及在发生故障之前进行风险评估
2026 年 11 月 14 日，香港时间 03:56 · 更新于 11 月 14 日，04:24 · 阅读时间 2 分钟
香港劳工处今日（11月14日）提醒雇主、承建商及雇员在大雨期间进行电力工作时应格外小心。该部门表示，雇主和承包商应避免指派工人执行电弧焊等电力任务，或在受暴风雨天气影响的地区处理电力装置。
该部门指出，即使在不直接暴露在雨中的地方，较高的湿度仍然存在触电风险。它敦促各方参考其发布的有关在恶劣天气和极端条件下安全工作的规范和指南。
劳工部列出了五项关键安全措施。其中包括确保电气系统的所有带电部件与电源隔离并在整个工作过程中保持断开；关闭并锁定电源，进行测试以确认电路已断电，显示适当的警告并在开始工作之前颁发工作许可证；确保保险丝和断路器等保护装置已安装并处于良好工作状态，并且便携式电动工具具有双重绝缘或正确接地；为工人提供绝缘手套和垫子等个人防护装备；如果带电工作不可避免，则要求有资格的人员进行全面的风险评估，并确保遵循所有适当的安全措施，以消除或控制电气危险。
员工还必须与雇主和承包商合作，遵守安全说明并使用安全设备。
劳工处已编制有关电力工作安全的安全指引及单张，可在辖下各区办事处免费索取或从劳工处网站（www.labour.gov.hk/tc/public/content2_8.htm）下载。有关职业安全及健康的查询，可致电2559 2297与该署联络。

Labour Dept warns employers, workers on electrical safety in rain | China Labour Bulletin Board
Saturday, 14 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
Labour Dept warns employers, workers on electrical safety in rain
Hong Kong's Labour Department urged employers and contractors to avoid assigning workers to electrical work in rain-hit areas, and to follow safety guidelines even in dry locations due to humid conditions. Measures include isolating power, using protective gear and conducting risk assessments before
14 Nov 2026 at 03:56 HKT · updated 14 Nov, 04:24 · 2 min read
Hong Kong's Labour Department today (14 November) reminded employers, contractors and employees to take extra precautions when carrying out electrical work during heavy rain. The department said employers and contractors should avoid assigning workers to perform electrical tasks, such as arc welding, or handle electrical installations in areas affected by stormy weather.
Even in locations not directly exposed to rain, the department noted that higher humidity still poses a risk of electric shock. It urged all parties to refer to its published codes and guides on working safely in adverse weather and extreme conditions.
The Labour Department listed five key safety measures. These include ensuring all live parts of the electrical system are isolated from the power source and kept disconnected throughout the work; switching off and locking the power supply, testing to confirm circuits are dead, displaying appropriate warnings and issuing a work permit before starting work; making sure protective devices such as fuses and circuit breakers are installed and in good working order, and that portable power tools are double-insulated or properly earthed; providing workers with personal protective equipment such as insulating gloves and mats; and, if live work is unavoidable, requiring a qualified person to conduct a full risk assessment and ensure all proper safety measures are followed to eliminate or control electrical hazards.
Employees are also required to cooperate with employers and contractors, follow safety instructions and use safety equipment.
The department has prepared safety guides and leaflets on electrical work safety, available free at its district offices or for download from its website (www.labour.gov.hk/tc/public/content2_8.htm). For enquiries on occupational safety and health, the department can be reached at 2559 2297.

title: All five defendants in San Po Kong subversion case intend to plead guilty, court hears

content:
两名男子因涉嫌在新蒲岗一栋工业大楼进行非法武器训练而被捕，他们向香港法院表示，他们打算承认共谋颠覆罪。湾仔区域法院。资料图片：HKFP。据当地媒体报道，学生邓毅博和服务员陈晓俊周四在区域法院出庭。辩方告诉陈士丹法官，两人计划认罪。两人是去年 12 月被指控串谋颠覆罪的五名被告之一。五人现已在法庭上表示他们打算认罪。法官表示，五人定于明年 3 月 15 日一起提出抗辩。在此之前，他们将继续被还押。据当地媒体报道，十月份，另外三名被告——学生黄杰伦、保安彭嘉良和保安李俊森——告诉法庭，他们将承认颠覆罪指控。黄还被指控持有儿童色情制品。检方10月在法庭上表示，已与辩方达成认罪协议：在黄承认颠覆罪后，持有儿童色情制品的指控将被存档。去年 12 月，唐和陈被指控时均为 23 岁。李当时26岁，彭24岁，黄21岁。2024年10月1日，人们在香港历史博物馆观看有关国家安全的视频装置。
图片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。检方指称，2024年11月1日至2025年12月11日期间，五名被告伙同及伙同其他不明人士，组织、策划、实施或参与以武力或以武力相威胁的行为，以颠覆国家政权、推翻香港特别行政区权力机构。根据第二十三条逮捕 这五人是去年12月11日和12月12日被捕的10人之一。警司周学贤表示，警方于 12 月 11 日持法院搜查令突击搜查新蒲岗工业大厦的一个单位，发现里面有 6 名男子，其中一名正在为其他人进行战斗训练。周说，警方缴获了五支气步枪、两支气手枪、五把军刀和一把长剑的仿制品，以及带有反政府标语的物品。他用粤语说：“此外，我们还发现了疑似爆炸物。”他补充说，警方爆炸品处理科正在检查这些物品。警方其后在大埔及油麻地拘捕另外三名男子。 12月12日，他们逮捕了一名妇女。所有这些人都是根据《维护国家安全条例》中的“非法钻探”条款被捕的，该条例是该市当地制定的安全立法，称为第 23 条。其中五人后来被指控串谋颠覆国家政权。

【原文 English Original】
Two men have told a Hong Kong court that they intend to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion after they were arrested on suspicion of illegal weapons training in an industrial building in San Po Kong. District Court in Wan Chai. File photo: HKFP. Student Tang Ngai-pok and waiter Chan Hiu-chun appeared at the District Court on Thursday, local media reported . The defence told Judge Stanley Chan that the duo planned to plead guilty to the charges. The two are among five defendants who were charged with conspiracy to commit subversion last December. All five have now stated in court that they intend to plead guilty. The judge said the five were set to enter their pleas together on March 15 next year. They will remain remanded in custody until then. In October, the other three defendants – student Wong Kit-lun, security guard Gallian Pang and security guard Lee Chun-sum – told the court that they would plead guilty to the subversion charges, local media reported . Wong was also charged with possession of child pornography. The prosecution said in court in October that a plea bargain had been reached with the defence: after Wong pleaded guilty to subversion, the charge of possession of child pornography would be left on file. Tang and Chan were both 23 years old when they were charged last December. Lee was 26 at the time, while Pang was 24 and Wong was 21. People watch a video installation on national security in the Hong Kong Museum of History, on October 1, 2024. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The prosecution alleged that between November 1, 2024 and December 11, 2025, the five defendants conspired together and with other persons unknown to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by force or threat of force with a view to subverting state power and overthrowing the body of power of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Arrests under Article 23 The five were among a group of 10 people who were arrested on December 11 and December 12 last year. Superintendent Chow Hok-yin said that officers raided a unit at the San Po Kong industrial building on December 11 with a court warrant and found six men inside, one providing combat training to the others. Officers seized five air rifles, two air pistols, replicas of five military knives and a long sword, as well as items bearing anti-government slogans, Chow said. “Additionally, we found objects suspected to be explosives,” he said in Cantonese, adding that the objects were being examined by the force’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal Bureau. Police later arrested another three men in Tai Po and Yau Ma Tei. On December 12, they arrested a woman. All of them were arrested under the “unlawful drilling” provision of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, the city’s locally enacted security legislation known as Article 23. Five were later charged with conspiracy to commit subversion.

content:
发言人办公室关于七国集团外长巴黎会议的联合声明 媒体报道 2026年11月13日，加拿大、法国、德国、意大利、日本、英国、美国等七国集团外长和欧盟高级代表发表以下声明。正文：2026 年 11 月 9 日至 10 日巴黎七国集团外长会议后的联合声明 我们，代表加拿大、法国、德国、意大利、日本、英国和美利坚合众国的七国集团外长，以及欧盟高级代表，于 2026 年 11 月 9 日至 10 日在巴黎举行的 2026 年七国集团主席国法国会议上举行会议。 乌克兰 我们重申对乌克兰及其勇敢人民的坚定支持他们捍卫自己的领土完整、主权、自由和独立。我们完全声援乌克兰人民，他们每天都遭受俄罗斯袭击，影响住宅楼、民用基础设施和文化遗产，以及针对乌克兰和其他伙伴的恶意混合活动。我们谴责黑海地区针对民用航运的袭击行动，这对全球粮食安全产生了重大影响，并加强了我们对保障粮食供应链的承诺。我们重申支持美国领导的通过直接和认真的谈判促进和平的持续努力。
我们重申了确保全面、全面和互惠停火的重要性。相互停止对所有能源基础设施和黑海的攻击，以保护平民，减少对能源（包括供暖、水和卫生设施以及粮食供应）的干扰，并支持全球市场的更大稳定，这是实现公正和持久和平的重要第一步。我们重申，有关欧洲未来安全的谈判必须包括欧洲人。正如我们在埃维昂七国集团峰会上所承诺的那样，我们评估了向乌克兰提供防空能力、系统和拦截器、远程能力和许可证方面取得的进展，这些能力将使其能够增加军事生产并行使其固有的自卫权。我们仍然致力于继续并加强朝这个方向的努力。我们承认需要以协调一致的方式解决乌克兰 2027 年及以后紧迫的融资需求，以支持乌克兰。我们谴责朝鲜和伊朗向俄罗斯提供军事援助，以及中国提供武器、军事训练和军民两用部件，这使得战争得以继续。我们明确表示打算继续对这些国家采取行动。基于我们领导人在埃维昂达成的共识，我们讨论了对俄罗斯战时经济日益增加的压力，包括通过制裁。
我们重申两国领导人承诺在针对俄罗斯的制裁问题上密切协调。我们重申决心重点关注悬挂假旗的船只或无国籍船只，以及保险公司、石油贸易商和中介机构等结构性推动者，以进一步扰乱和威慑用于规避制裁的影子舰队。我们重申支持乌克兰能源安全和恢复力，决定加大资金和物资支持力度，帮助乌克兰度过冬季。我们欢迎为使切尔诺贝利新安全隔离设施的修复保持在国际议程上的高度重视而做出的努力

Office of the Spokesman Joint Statement on the G7 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Paris Media Note November 13, 2026 The following statement was released by the G7 Foreign Ministers of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States of America and the High Representative of the European Union. Begin Text: Joint declaration following the G7 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Paris on 9 and 10 November 2026 We, the G7 Foreign Ministers representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America, along with the High Representative of the European Union, met under the 2026 French G7 Presidency in Paris, on 9 and 10 November 2026. Ukraine We reaffirmed our unwavering support to Ukraine and its courageous people as they defend their territorial integrity, sovereignty, freedom, and independence. We stand in full solidarity with the Ukrainian population suffering from daily Russian attacks affecting residential buildings, civilian infrastructure, and cultural heritage, as well as malicious hybrid activities against Ukraine and other partners. We condemned the campaign of strikes carried out against civilian shipping in the Black Sea area, which have significant consequences on global food security, and strengthened our commitment to safeguarding food supply chains. We reiterated our support to ongoing U.S.-led efforts to facilitate peace through direct and serious negotiations. We reaffirmed the importance of securing a full, comprehensive, and reciprocal ceasefire. A reciprocal halt to attacks on all energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea to protect civilians, reduce disruption to energy, including heating, water and sanitation, and food supply and support greater stability in global markets is an important first step towards just and lasting peace. We reiterated that negotiations on the future security of Europe must include the Europeans. As we pledged during the G7 Summit in Évian, we took stock of progress on supplying Ukraine with air defense capabilities, systems and interceptors, long-range capabilities and licenses that will allow it to increase its military production and to exercise its inherent right of self-defense. We remain committed to continuing and strengthening our efforts in this direction. We acknowledged the need to address Ukraine’s pressing financing needs for 2027 and beyond in a coordinated way to support Ukraine. We condemned the provision of military assistance to Russia by North Korea and Iran, and the provision of weapons, military training and dual-use components by China, which enables the continuation of the war. We made clear our intention to continue to take action against these countries. Building on the consensus among our leaders in Évian, we discussed increasing pressure on Russia’s war economy, including through sanctions. We reaffirmed the commitment of our leaders to closely coordinate on sanctions against Russia. We reiterated our determination to focus on ships flying false flags or stateless ships, as well as structural enablers, such as insurers, oil traders, and intermediaries, to further disrupt and deter shadow fleet vessels used to circumvent sanctions. We reaffirmed our support to Ukraine’s energy security and resilience, and decided to step up our financial and material support to help the country get through the winter. We welcomed efforts to keep the repair of the Chornobyl New Safe Confinement high on the international agenda, as demonstrated by the donors’ conference organized in Paris on 9 November by France, EBRD, and Ukraine. We also welcomed the ongoing projects coordinated through the Tallinn Mechanism under Italy’s Chairpersonship to support Ukraine’s civilian cyber resilience. Middle East On Iran, we commended the work of the regional mediators and reiterated our support for all diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a lasting settlement that addresses international concerns over Iran’s nuclear program and contributes to regional security. We reiterated that Iran must never be allowed to develop or acquire a nuclear weapon. We urged Iran to stop its support for nonstate armed groups in the region. Absent a diplomatic solution, we committed to continuing our coordination to economically and politically constrain the Iranian regime’s ability to sow instability in the region and around the world. We strongly condemned Iran’s attacks against its neighbors and the disruption of international trade, energy security, and the global economy caused by the obstruction of transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz. We reaffirmed the importance of protecting civilians and civilian objects, and called on Iran to respect its international human rights and humanitarian law obligations. We called on Iran to cease its persistent attacks against civilian vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. We reaffirmed our commitment to the right of safe and free passage and our opposition to any tolls, fees, illegal costs, discriminations or any limitation imposed on maritime transit through the Strait. We underscored the importance of the defensive activities undertaken by U.S. Central Command in the Strait of Hormuz to demine the waterway and escort civilian vessels. We recognized that the multinational, independent, and defensive initiative led by France and the UK can play an important role in facilitating the resumption of maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz also by supporting the verification of the removal of all mines. We reaffirmed our commitment to fully implement the obligations under all relevant UN Security Council resolutions sanctions and related restrictive measures reinstated in September 2025 through the snapback mechanism under UN Security Council resolution 2231, and called on all UN Member States to do the same. We urged Iran to return to compliance with its international obligations, and in particular to resume full cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in order to restore transparency regarding the nature of its nuclear program. We also expressed grave concern over Iranian involvement in violent plots against many of our citizens and territories. We recognized the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September. Iran should be in no doubt that we are united and remain committed to safeguarding our sovereignty. On Yemen, we condemned in the strongest terms the unacceptable continued strikes carried out by the Houthis in Yemen and against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including those on civilians and civilian infrastructure. We called on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions and threats and refrain from any further escalation to enable a return to an inclusive political process. We expressed our solidarity with the Government of Yemen and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and reaffirmed their right to defend their security, sovereignty and territorial integrity in accordance with international law. We urged all actors, including Iran, to end their arming of and support for the Houthis, in violation of several United Nations Security Council resolutions. We expressed deep concern at the worsening humanitarian impact of the conflict and called for the protection of civilians and safe, unimpeded humanitarian access with the urgent opening of a humanitarian corridor in Taiz. We reiterated our call for the immediate and unconditional release of all humanitarian personnel, including the 70 UN staff who remain unjustly detained by the Houthis. We reaffirmed the importance of maritime safety and security in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. We shared the importance of continuing support to the Government of Yemen, including through capacity-building. We recognized the positive contribution of the EU maritime defensive operations EUNAVFOR ASPIDES and EUNAVFOR ATALANTA to restore maritime security and protect maritime shipping and the lives of seafarers in the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. On Lebanon, we stressed the need for all parties to fully respect the ceasefire and expressed support for implementation of the Trilateral Framework and of UN Security Council Resolution 1701. We reiterated that the disarmament of all non-state armed groups, foremost among them Hezbollah, remains essential to ensuring that all weapons are brought under the authority and control of the Lebanese state. We called on Lebanon and Israel to make progress implementing the pilot zones to allow for full and verifiable Hezbollah disarmament and Israeli redeployment as the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) deploy. We reiterated our support for the Lebanese authorities’ efforts to achieve the disarmament of all non-state armed groups and for Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. As the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) is set to expire at the end of the year, we underscored the need for a robust, credible, and long-lasting security architecture in Lebanon in support of the LAF, in line with UN Security Council resolution 1701 and enabling further implementation of the Trilateral Framework. In calling for a strengthened LAF, we welcomed the establishment of the EU CSDP mission EU Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon). We called upon Lebanese actors to move forward in the adoption and implementation of financial reforms in view of agreeing on an IMF program. On Gaza, we remained committed to the swift implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 2803 and to accelerate humanitarian, recovery and reconstruction efforts aimed at fostering long-term stability. We unequivocally condemned the attacks committed by Hamas on the 7th of October, reiterating that Hamas can have no role in Gaza’s future and must decommission its weaponry. Israel must progressively withdraw from the Gaza Strip, under the conditions outlined in UN Security Council Resolution 2803. We stressed the urgent need for the safe, rapid, sustained, and unimpeded delivery of humanitarian assistance throughout Gaza and the opening of additional crossings, as well as the rehabilitation of humanitarian infrastructure and the protection of civilians. It is vital that all parties continue to engage constructively on the next steps outlined in the Comprehensive Plan, in pursuit of a political horizon for peaceful and prosperous coexistence, for the Israeli and Palestinian people, that advances Middle East peace and stability. We called for ending terrorist attacks and other actions which increase tensions and the risk of escalation in the West Bank. On Syria, we reaffirmed our strong support for a peaceful and inclusive political transition towards a united, sovereign and stable Syria, ensuring respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all Syrians. We stressed the importance of fully implementing the arrangements reached on the peaceful integration of Northeast Syria and reiterated our commitment to fighting terrorism. We expressed concern over the situation in Southern Syria, calling for the protection of civilians and respect for Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. We also reaffirmed the importance of supporting Syria’s economic recovery and reconstruction to achieve lasting stability and to enhance regional connectivity. Indo-Pacific We emphasised the importance of a free and open Indo-Pacific region which is prosperous and secure, and that protects shared principles including sovereignty, territorial integrity, the rule of law, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. We reiterated our commitment to upholding freedom of navigation and overflight in the region and called on States to abide by their obligations under international law, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). We expressed our serious concerns over the situation in the East China Sea and the South China Sea. We reaffirmed our strong opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo, particularly by force or coercion or any actions that raise tensions and risk escalation. We reiterated that the award rendered by the Arbitral Tribunal on 12 July 2016 is a significant milestone, which is final and legally binding upon the parties to the proceedings. We stressed the importance of maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. In the context of China’s increasingly assertive activities in the waters east of Taiwan, which threaten regional stability, freedom of navigation and the safety of international shipping, we reaffirmed our opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo, particularly by force or coercion, or the threat thereof. We encouraged the peaceful resolution of cross-Strait issues through constructive dialogue. We also expressed our support for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in international organizations. We strongly condemned North Korea’s unlawful nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs and reaffirmed our commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea, in accordance with all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. We underlined that increased cooperation between Russia and North Korea has serious consequences for European and Indo-Pacific security. We urged North Korea to immediately cease all assistance and to withdraw its troops. We reaffirmed our concern regarding cryptocurrency thefts and cybercrimes committed by North Korea and expressed the need to respond to its unlawful overseas labor program. We urged North Korea to immediately resolve the issue of abductions. We remain deeply concerned by the deterioration of the human rights and humanitarian situation across Myanmar. We reiterated the need for the immediate de-escalation of violence, the unimpeded passage of humanitarian assistance, and a genuine and inclusive democratic process that reflects the will of the people of Myanmar. Sudan We were alarmed by the devastating consequences of the war on the Sudanese people and the growing risk of famine in parts of Darfur and Kordofan. Continued fighting, restrictions on humanitarian access and attacks, including by drones, affecting healthcare facilities, displacement camps and the infrastructure civilians rely on for food are putting lives at risk, which is being compounded by the impact of El Niño. A year after the atrocities in El Fasher, we unequivocally condemned all violations and abuses against civilians, including conflict-related sexual violence against women and girls. We called on all external actors to cease supplying or facilitating armed, logistical, and financial support to the belligerents and to use their influence to encourage the warring parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, lift restrictions on humanitarian access and support de-escalation, and avoid any action that could contribute to the conflict. We underscored that, beyond an immediate cease-fire, a peaceful and durable resolution of the conflict is essential to securing unity and long-term stability in Sudan. In line with the principles stated at the Sudan Ministerial Conference in Berlin in April this year, we reaffirmed that a credible Sudanese civilian-led, inclusive, and transparent political dialogue process that addresses historical grievances and respects Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is critical to securing a lasting peace. We demanded the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces comply with international humanitarian law, engage in negotiations including with the Quad with a view to reaching a permanent ceasefire, and guarantee rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. We reiterated our full support to the work of the Quintet aiming to facilitate such a dialogue, in a process that should run in parallel to and in close alignment with efforts to secure a ceasefire. We call on the wider international community to support these efforts. Horn of Africa We noted with great concern the worsening security situation in the Horn of Africa, specifically between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which bears the risk of regional escalation amid rising cross-border tensions. We underlined the serious consequences further escalation could have for regional stability, already dire humanitarian crises, security and international trade, including in the Red Sea. We called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint, pursue diplomatic solutions, and ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access and the protection of civilians, especially women and children. We reaffirmed the importance of respecting the sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity of all countries in the region. In particular, we supported efforts by the United Nations and the African Union to reduce tensions and to facilitate dialogue between the parties. Haiti We supported and welcomed the renewal of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) mandate through March 2027, which aims to assist Haitian forces in restoring security and stability in Haiti. We also welcomed the renewal of the UN sanctions regime, which promotes accountability for individuals and entities who threaten peace, security, and stability in Haiti. We called for international support to strengthen the Haitian National Police and Haitian Armed Forces, uphold the rule of law, and combat impunity. We also called on all security actors operating in Haiti to prioritize the protection of Haitian civilians in all security operations. We stressed the importance of organizing democratic elections in Haiti and noted the postponement of the first round of elections to July 2027. Noting progress made by the government and the Provisional Electoral Council in their work to advance Haiti’s path to elected governance, we underlined the need to safeguard the credibility and integrity of the electoral process and underscored the responsibility of Haitian authorities to ensure their full and impartial implementation of the electoral decree. We called for concrete results that strengthen public confidence in the electoral process and contribute to a credible return to democratic governance. We noted with concerns regarding the participation of sanctioned individuals in the political process, which undermines accountability and public trust. The people of Haiti have a right to determine their future through credible democratic processes and leaders who serve the public interest with integrity. We remain deeply concerned by the ongoing humanitarian crisis, widespread violence, and reports of human rights violations in Haiti. We urged the international community to intensify financial contributions to the UN Trust Fund, recognizing that the success of the UN-mandated hybrid mission depends on sustained multilateral support to resource its operations. We urged critical international support for humanitarian assistance for Haiti, in order to address the multiple crises facing the people of Haiti. We also underscored the importance of laying the groundwork for Haiti’s economic recovery with the support of international financial institutions and other multilateral partners. We welcomed the World Bank’s Compact with the Haitian authorities as a common framework to assess Haitian-led reform efforts and strengthen accountability for results. We committed to working with diverse Haitian and international partners to promote greater coordination and complementarity of efforts. Cuba We expressed our concerns about the profound economic crisis and humanitarian needs facing the Cuban people, including shortages of food, fuel and medicines. We stressed the importance of improving humanitarian aid delivery mechanisms into and throughout Cuba in order to improve the welfare of the Cuban people. We called on the Cuban authorities to pursue and implement significant and meaningful political and economic reforms to advance prosperity, respect for human rights, and the legitimate aspirations of the Cuban people, and to take concrete steps towards multi-party democratic governance, press freedom, and freedom of expression and association. We also called on the Cuban authorities to release all individuals who have been arbitrarily detained. We encouraged constructive and inclusive dialogue in order to find a way out of the crisis. Venezuela We acknowledged the will of the people of Venezuela to turn the page on the country’s prolonged political and economic crisis. In this regard, we reaffirmed our full support for the ongoing reconciliation talks that bring together the interim government and the delegation representing the National Assembly elected in 2015 and which have already yielded measurable progress. We called on all parties to continue to engage in good faith on the path leading from the restoration of institutions and the rule of law to the holding of free and fair elections. We emphasised the particular importance of providing guarantees to all parties and civil society organizations to enable their participation in the democratic process. We called for the release of all political prisoners. We acknowledged that Venezuela’s economic recovery is inextricably linked to the political reconciliation process and encouraged investments and commercial deals that help build a more stable and prosperous future for the Venezuelan people. We also offered emergency humanitarian response and civil protection activities following the devastating twin earthquakes on June 24, 2026. UN reform and efficiency of humanitarian assistance Committed to making the UN more efficient and effective, accountable and impactful, we welcomed ongoing efforts under the UN80, as well as humanitarian reform initiatives, including the Humanitarian Reset. These latter initiatives aim to strengthen the humanitarian system through better coordination, mandate delineation, and consolidation of common services and critical enablers, while remaining fully open to all impartial humanitarian actors and in full compliance with international law and the UN Charter. We reiterated the importance of maintaining sustained momentum in driving forward reform at this critical juncture for the UN. We commended the work of the G7 working group on the efficiency of the humanitarian supply chain (LOG+7), which is one of the most strategic drivers to increase the impact of assistance in a context of a significant decrease in financing and worsening of crises. These efforts towards a more integrated supply chain, including the reinforcement of the existing humanitarian hubs and pooling of resources, will help reach a greater proportion of the population in need without budgetary changes, and thereby contributing to address growing humanitarian needs including food insecurity and malnutrition in all its forms. This work will continue within the framework of the Humanitarian Leadership Group on Supply Chain led by the European Union and through the UN80 integrated supply chain initiative. Food security and nutrition We stressed our commitment to food security and nutrition to address the consequences of conflicts and instability, and to strengthen food systems resilience. We called for continuing action to address the disruptions to food trade in the Black Sea in the context of the war in Ukraine, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the El Niño phenomenon. Together, in 2026, we mobilized 2.5 billion USD of international funding to address the crisis in the Middle East, adding to our long-term commitment to more resilient food systems and fertilizer markets. Forced displacement of people We noted the serious impact of conflict, violence, and instability on affected countries and regions, as well as on broader regional and international security affecting the security of civilian populations. This constitutes a driver of forced displacement and irregular migration, and exposes victims of human trafficking to acute forms of abuse and exploitation. Malicious hybrid activities We condemned persistent malicious hybrid activities by states and non-state actors aimed at undermining the security and stability of the G7 Members and partner countries, through coordinated and deliberate campaigns, including acts of sabotage against critical infrastructure, malicious cyber activities, foreign information manipulation and interference, and the instrumentalization of migration. Such actions risk unintended effects, escalation, and miscalculation. We reaffirmed our determination to act resolutely and in a coordinated manner to address hybrid campaigns, using all available tools to prevent, deter, and respond to these actions, irrespective of their origin, scale and intensity. We stressed the need to reinforce our common efforts and accelerate work on all relevant work strands, in order to strengthen resilience, enhance preparedness, and protect critical infrastructure. Transnational Organized Crime We expressed concern about the increasingly sophisticated methods, violence, and reach of transnational organized criminal groups worldwide, in particular those involved in drug trafficking, human trafficking, and migrant smuggling, and underscored the importance of international cooperation to strengthen maritime security, combat illicit trafficking networks, and dismantle these groups. We also recognized that online scams are a form of rapidly growing transnational organized crime that poses a threat to regional and international peace and security, and stressed the need to strengthen collaboration, including with the private sector, as appropriate, and to disrupt online scam networks, which may be linked to other forms of transnational organized crime. Maritime and port security We reaffirmed the absolute necessity of ensuring maritime safety and security, and of safeguarding freedom of navigation worldwide, in accordance with international law as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), in order to prevent any lasting disruption to global supply chains, particularly with regard to energy, fertilizers and food products, because this can seriously affect vulnerable economies and populations. We recalled the global pledge initiated by the EU of 12 October 2026 on maintaining the integrity of the international law of the sea “No Fees, No Tolls”. We also underlined the need to strengthen the resilience and protection of critical undersea infrastructure, particularly submarine energy infrastructure and telecommunications cables, and their landing stations, including through enhanced international cooperation, information-sharing, redundancy and rapid repair capabilities. We encouraged practical cooperation with industry to improve access to repair vessels, equipment and spare parts, and to facilitate timely authorizations and port access for repairs, consistent with applicable international law and national requirements. In order to strengthen operational cooperation across our key maritime ports or relevant authorities, we, together with Brazil and the Republic of Korea, launched the G7+ Ports Network to Combat Drug Trafficking. This network will help strengthen operational cooperation, the exchange of information and the sharing of best practices to protect our ports from drug trafficking, in coordination and coherence with existing initiatives such as the European Ports Alliance, the European Coalition Against Drugs and the Maritime Safety Committee, and with the support of international organizations, in particular the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. We welcomed the work of the members of the G7++ “Friends of the Gulf of Guinea” group to create opportunities for deeper engagement with the Yaoundé Architecture for strengthening partnerships in the fields of training, capacity-building and joint operations, as well as our judicial cooperation to facilitate the prosecution of traffickers apprehended at sea. We welcomed the work carried out by the members of the G7 and Nordic Baltic 8++ Shadow Fleet Task Force and reiterated our commitment to enhance G7 coordination with partners to further disrupt and deter the global shadow fleet engaged in illegal, unsafe or environmentally perilous activities. Resilience of critical satellite infrastructure We also recognized the need to strengthen the resilience of critical satellite infrastructure, including satellites, ground stations and control centres, and their supporting terrestrial connections and power supplies. We encouraged stronger protection against physical and cyber threats and harmful interference, as well as redundancy and contingency arrangements to maintain essential services. Taking into account the interdependence of undersea, satellite and terrestrial networks, we encouraged cooperation among competent authorities and operators on risk assessment, timely and secure incident information-sharing, and preparedness exercises. Such cooperation should support rapid service restoration, including through complementary connectivity options for essential communications, while safeguarding sensitive information. Frontier models We recognized the opportunities offered by frontier models to advance science and strengthen our economies, while also noting the need to ensure the secure and trustworthy development of these advanced systems and models through adequate safeguards and human-centric adoption, taking into account that they can pose risks, including for society and economic security. We acknowledged that frontier models can be misused by state and non-state malicious actors, including for malicious cyber activities and criminal activities, or to acquire and enhance chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or explosive capabilities. We recognized the importance of strengthening the security and resilience of frontier models to advance innovation, economic prosperity, and national security. The developments and issues are complex. That is why it is key that governments, international organizations businesses and academia engage in discussions on model adoption. We will pursue our discussion to advance a secure innovation ecosystem for trusted frontier model deployment including through efforts started with the Hiroshima AI Process. Economic security and critical minerals We reaffirmed our shared concerns regarding the use of non-market policies and practices and economic coercion, especially on critical minerals and their related dual-use items. We will work towards strengthening our competitiveness and addressing the root causes of our common challenges. We affirmed the importance of the G7 Coordination Platform on Economic Coercion to build a common response to economic coercion and further promote cooperation with partners beyond the G7. We further recognized the importance of maintaining and strengthening of our midstream and downstream industries’ competitiveness, including in relation to critical minerals, by protecting critical technologies and commit to working within the G7 and with partners to coordinate on policy measures for technology control. Recognizing the strategic role of critical minerals value chains for the economic prosperity and security of our countries, and in light of the high market concentration in certain economies in the critical minerals sector, we reiterated the urgency of reducing strategic dependencies and vulnerabilities by diversifying and securing trusted supply chains to build up our collective resilience. In that regard, we recognized the importance of the measures announced at the Evian Summit to ensure critical minerals supply chains resilience and security. We commended the expansion of the G7 Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance which builds on the G7 Critical Minerals Production Alliance launched under Canada’s G7 Presidency in 2025. This expanded Alliance and other platforms provide a venue for cooperation within the G7 and with partner countries in order to facilitate discussion, support data-driven decision-making and foster coordination among members to strengthen diversification and resilience of critical minerals value chains. End Text.

title: How Shanghai fund manager Kang Wei introduced his wife Alice Huang to Jensen and built $7.5 billion Nvidia AI GPU smuggling operation
